metadata.title: Efficient Computation of Positional Population Counts Using SIMD Instructions

extraction_notes.note: The C++ listings in figures (CSA, CSA_AVX512, the 256 B and 1 kB circuits, the scalar baseline, the vectorized increment, and the inline scalar loop) are code, not prose; they were not made nodes. The algorithms they implement are the prose algorithm nodes AP3-AP6.
The experimental evidence is a table of cycles, instructions and GB/s per input size (tab:results) and a speed figure; only the findings stated in prose became numerical claims.

The abstract and the conclusion restate the problem, the speedups and the near-memcpy speed; per one node per repeated statement they got no node. The headline speedup factor is inconsistent across copies: 50-fold (abstract, intro), over 40 times (conclusion); instruction reduction 400 times (abstract, 4.1) vs 300 times measured (ClP22).

PP2 has index typos: it calls $B_0,\ldots,B_N$ the first $N$ outputs and writes the following inputs as $d_N,\ldots$ (should start at $d_{2^N}$). AP5 says it uses the 256 B circuit but feeds 512 B blocks and reads a fourth register B3, which matches the 512 B circuit.

AP3 is introduced as an illustration ('Let us illustrate this approach'), so it could be an example; chose algorithm because it is a stepwise procedure. PP2 is a recursive circuit construction that could be an algorithm; chose proof because it is the argument for ClP6.
An empirical performance statement of prior work (Mula et al.) stated in full; typed theorem/external per the cited-result rule though claim would read more naturally.

nodes.name: population count
nodes.statement: In many applications such as deep learning\cite{Dai2017,Courbariaux2016,Zhang2018,Hubara2016}, indexing\cite{Lemire2016}, chemistry\cite{Haque2011}, cryptography\cite{Sanyal2018}, and bioinformatics\cite{Layer2016,Danek2018,Wu2010,Purcell2007} it is desirable to compute the number of set bits in a computer word. This operation is referred to as the population count (\texttt{popcnt}), Hamming weight, or the sideways sum of the word.
nodes.genus: the number of set bits in a computer word
nodes.statement_short: The population count (popcnt, Hamming weight, sideways sum) of a word is its number of set bits.

nodes.name: population count of 100100100
nodes.statement: For example, the machine word \texttt{\underline{1}00\underline{1}00\underline{1}0} has a population count of three since there are three set bits.

nodes.name: SIMD instructions
nodes.statement: We have previously described efficient subroutines for computing the population count\cite{mula2017faster} of large arrays that takes advantage of SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) instructions available on most commodity processors. These instructions operate on wide data registers and reduce the number of instructions required by processing multiple machine words simultaneously.
nodes.statement_short: SIMD instructions operate on wide registers, processing several machine words per instruction.

nodes.name: one-hot encoding
nodes.statement: It is common to represent categorical variables using one-hot (1-of-$k$) encoding\cite{lippert2013exhaustive,mittag2015influence} where each categorical value maps to a corresponding bit within a $k$-bit word and each word may only have a single bit set.
nodes.origin_citation: Lippert et al. 2013; Mittag et al. 2015
differentia: each categorical value maps to a corresponding bit within a $k$-bit word
each word may only have a single bit set

nodes.name: one-hot encoding of countries
nodes.statement: As an illustrative example, consider a categorical variable \texttt{country} that has the eight distinct values \texttt{Australia}, \texttt{Canada}, \texttt{China}, \texttt{France}, \texttt{Japan}, \texttt{Portugal}, \texttt{Spain}, and \texttt{USA}. These categorical string values can be unambiguously dictionary-compressed into one-hot encodings (Table~\ref{table:one-hotexample}) resulting in lower memory usage and more efficient queries.
nodes.statement_short: Eight country names are dictionary-compressed into 8-bit one-hot words.

nodes.name: frequency histogram
nodes.statement: In this context, we want to compute the frequency histogram, that is the number of occurrences of each value.
nodes.genus: the number of occurrences of each value

nodes.name: country frequency histogram
nodes.statement: For example, given a stream (Table~\ref{table:one-hotexample-stream}) of one-hot encoded values (Table~\ref{table:one-hotexample}), we want to compute the number of times each country has been observed such that \texttt{France} has been observed three times, \texttt{Portugal} two times, \texttt{USA} four times, and \texttt{China} one time.
nodes.statement_short: A stream of one-hot country words yields counts France 3, Portugal 2, USA 4, China 1.

nodes.name: positional population count
nodes.statement: We name this novel generalization of the population count operation to individual bits spanning multiple words as the \textit{positional population count} (\texttt{pospopcnt}). If each word is made of $k$-bits then we want to compute $k$~counts representing the total number of set bits at each of the $k$~positions.
nodes.genus: generalization of the population count operation
differentia: we want to compute $k$~counts representing the total number of set bits at each of the $k$~positions
nodes.statement_short: For a stream of $k$-bit words, pospopcnt returns the $k$ counts of set bits at each bit position.

nodes.name: per-word vs positional population count
nodes.statement: As an illustrative example, consider three given input words $A$, $B$, and $C$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:introduction}), the conventional per-word population count computes the number of set bits for each word independently (Fig.~\ref{fig:introductionpane2}). In contrast, the positional population count operation computes the \emph{vertical} population count over these words for independent bit positions (Fig.~\ref{fig:introductionpane1}).
nodes.statement_short: On three words, popcnt counts bits per word while pospopcnt counts vertically per bit position.

nodes.name: AVX-512
nodes.statement: The AVX-512 family of ISAs can operate on up to thirty-two 512-bit registers.
differentia: can operate on up to thirty-two 512-bit registers

nodes.name: 50-fold speedup over scalar
nodes.statement: Notably, we show that our proposed algorithm can be in excess of 50-fold faster compared to a baseline scalar approach, as long as the input is sufficiently large (several kilobytes).
conclusions: our proposed algorithm can be in excess of 50-fold faster compared to a baseline scalar approach
assumptions: as long as the input is sufficiently large (several kilobytes)

nodes.name: Wilkes-Wheeler-Gill population-count
nodes.statement: One of the earliest efficient algorithm to compute the population count is the Wilkes-Wheeler-Gill population-count\cite{Wilkes} (Fig.~\ref{fig:tree-of-adders}). This algorithm begins by adding adjacent bits into two-bit subwords, then adds these two-bit subwords into four-bit subwords, and finally adds adjacent four-bit subwords into byte values. These byte values are then summed using a multiplication and a bit-shift. It has a natural tree structure and can be described as a "tree of adders"\cite{KnuthV4A}.
nodes.statement_short: Tree of adders: sum adjacent bits into 2-bit, then 4-bit, then byte subwords, and combine bytes by a multiplication and a shift.

nodes.name: Harley-Seal algorithm
nodes.statement: Another efficient approach\cite{warren2007} is the Harley-Seal algorithm that is based on carry-save adder (CSA) networks frequently used in hardware microarchitectures.
nodes.statement_short: Population count via carry-save adder (CSA) networks.

nodes.name: carry-save adder (CSA) subroutine
nodes.statement: The CSA subroutine takes three input words and produce two output words: (1) a sequence of partial sum bits, and (2) a sequence of carry bits.
differentia: takes three input words and produce two output words: (1) a sequence of partial sum bits, and (2) a sequence of carry bits

nodes.name: bitwise full-adder formulas
nodes.statement: Given three~bit values ($a,b,c\in \{0,1\}$), the sum $a + b + c$ is computed as a 2-bit word where the least significant bit is given by $(a\mathrm{xor} b) \mathrm{xor} c$ and the most significant bit is given by $(a \mathrm{bitand} b) \mathrm{bitor} ( (a \mathrm{xor} b) \mathrm{bitand} c )$.
conclusions: the least significant bit is given by $(a\mathrm{xor} b) \mathrm{xor} c$
the most significant bit is given by $(a \mathrm{bitand} b) \mathrm{bitor} ( (a \mathrm{xor} b) \mathrm{bitand} c )$
nodes.statement_short: The 2-bit sum $a+b+c$ has LSB $a\oplus b\oplus c$ and MSB $(a\wedge b)\vee((a\oplus b)\wedge c)$.

nodes.name: proof that a CSA needs 5 operations
nodes.statement: We reuse the $a \mathrm{xor} b$ expression from the computation of the least significant bit when computing the most significant bit.
nodes.statement_short: Direct count: sharing the $a \oplus b$ subexpression between the two output bits.

nodes.name: CSA uses 5 logical operations
nodes.statement: Therefore, three values can be summed using 5~logical operations.
conclusions: three values can be summed using 5~logical operations

nodes.name: four-input CSA circuit
nodes.statement: Let us illustrate this approach by computing the population count of four inputs words using a simplified circuit (Fig.~\ref{fig:hsillustration}). Starting with two 64-bit words initialized to zero: one for the least significant bits ($B_0$) and one for the second least significant bits ($B_1$). \begin{enumerate} \item Two input words are summed with $B_0$ using a CSA subroutine (Fig.~\ref{fig:csacpp}) resulting in two outputs: one corresponding to the least significant bits stored in $B_0$ and another corresponding to the second most significant bit: let us call it $x$. \item Two new input words are summed with $B_0$ using the same CSA subroutine. Again the output corresponding to the least significant bit is stored in $B_0$. We have a second output corresponding to the second most significant bits, let us call it $y$. \item In the final step, $x$, $y$, and $B_1$ are added together. The output corresponding to the least significant bits is stored in $B_1$. Similarly, the output corresponding to the most significant bit is stored in $B_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Harley-Seal circuit on four words: two CSAs into $B_0$ produce carries $x,y$, a third CSA adds $x,y,B_1$ giving $B_1,B_2$.

nodes.name: population count from CSA outputs
nodes.statement: If $c_i$ is the population count of $B_i$, then the population count of the four words is $1 c_0 + 2 c_1 + 4 c_2$.
conclusions: the population count of the four words is $1 c_0 + 2 c_1 + 4 c_2$

nodes.name: CSA circuit on 2^N words
nodes.statement: In general, given $2^N$~input words, we can produce $N+1$~words corresponding to the sum of the bits using a CSA circuit. Then the per-word population count can be computed from the resulting $N$~words.
conclusions: we can produce $N+1$~words corresponding to the sum of the bits using a CSA circuit
nodes.statement_short: A CSA circuit compresses $2^N$ words into $N+1$ bit-sliced sum words from which the population count follows.

nodes.name: circuit function F_N
nodes.statement: Assume that we have a circuit that takes $2^N$~inputs as well as $B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1}$ and produces the updated $B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$ corresponding to the sum. We can represent this circuit as a function $F_N (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^N-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1})$ that outputs $B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: $F_N$ maps $2^N$ inputs and running sums $B_0..B_{N-1}$ to updated $B_0..B_N$.

nodes.name: recursive doubling construction of CSA circuits
nodes.statement: We can then construct a larger circuit that takes twice as many inputs by two calls to the circuit together with an additional CSA routine. Indeed, to compute $F_{N+1} (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^{N+1}-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N})$, we can start by computing $F_N (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^N-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1})$. We provide the first $N$~outputs ($B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$) from this first call to $F_N$ to a second call to the circuit $F_N$, this time using the $2^N$ following inputs $d_N, \ldots, d_{2^{N+1}-1}$. We are left with three values $B_N$, one was provided as an input to $F_{N+1}$, and two have been produced by a call to the smaller circuit $F_N$. We can combine these with a CSA routine.
nodes.statement_short: Recursive construction: $F_{N+1}$ is two calls to $F_N$ followed by one CSA combining the three $B_N$ values.

nodes.name: 2^N-1 CSAs suffice for 2^N inputs
nodes.statement: By such a recursive argument, we can show that $2^N-1$~CSA routines is sufficient to process $2^N$~inputs.
conclusions: $2^N-1$~CSA routines is sufficient to process $2^N$~inputs

nodes.name: SIMD CSA network is fastest population count
nodes.statement: Given sufficiently large input arrays (e.g., 1\,kB), such a SIMD-accelerated CSA network is superior to all known population count alternatives on current Intel processors\cite{mula2017faster}.
conclusions: such a SIMD-accelerated CSA network is superior to all known population count alternatives on current Intel processors

nodes.name: AVX-512 CSA in two instructions
nodes.statement: On processors with the AVX-512 instruction set architecture available, we can simplify this subroutine down to two instructions by using the three-operand instruction \texttt{vpternlogd} using the \texttt{\_mm512\_ternarylogic\_epi32} intrinsic function (Fig.~\ref{fig:csa-avx512}).
assumptions: On processors with the AVX-512 instruction set architecture available
conclusions: we can simplify this subroutine down to two instructions by using the three-operand instruction \texttt{vpternlogd}
nodes.statement_short: With AVX-512's vpternlogd, a CSA needs only two instructions.

nodes.name: vpternlogd instruction
nodes.statement: The \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction operates on three input bits $a$, $b$, $c$ and an 8-bit sequence $i$ and returns the bit at index $1a + 2b + 4c$ of $i$. Given three 512-bit input registers, the instructions generates a 512-bit output, executing 512-bit operations in parallel.
differentia: operates on three input bits $a$, $b$, $c$ and an 8-bit sequence $i$ and returns the bit at index $1a + 2b + 4c$ of $i$
nodes.statement_short: vpternlogd returns bit $a+2b+4c$ of an 8-bit immediate, bitwise over 512-bit registers.

nodes.name: vpternlogd computes any ternary Boolean function
nodes.statement: The \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction can compute any ternary Boolean function using a single instruction.
conclusions: can compute any ternary Boolean function using a single instruction

nodes.name: derivation of vpternlogd immediates
nodes.statement: This instruction is useful in computing the most and least significant bits in the CSA routine. To determine the value of the 8-bit sequence $i$ in the context of computing the least and most significant bits, it suffices to enumerate all 8~possible inputs (Table~\ref{tab:csatern}). \begin{itemize} \item The least significant bit can be computed as the \texttt{xor} of the three inputs. Therefore, the \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction computes the desired output when the bits at index $\{1, 2, 4, 7\}$ of $i$ are set. In software, this bit sequence is represented as the integer 0b10010110 in binary or 150 in decimal. \item Computing the most significant bits involves the expression $(a \mathrm{~and~} b) \mathrm{~or~} ((a \mathrm{~xor~} b) \mathrm{~and~} c$. We can achieve this result by setting the bits at index \{3, 5, 6, 7\} of $i$ that can be represented as the binary string 0b11101000 or 232 in decimal.
nodes.statement_short: Truth-table enumeration of the 8 inputs gives immediates 150 (xor, LSB) and 232 (majority, MSB).

nodes.name: gain factor computation
nodes.statement: When comparing the resulting AVX-512 routine to its 64-bit equivalent (Fig.~\ref{fig:csacpp}), we observe that the AVX-512-based CSA subroutine can process 8~times as many bits (512 versus 64) while simultaneously reducing the number of logical operations from 5 to 2.
nodes.statement_short: Direct arithmetic: 8 times wider registers and 2 instead of 5 operations.

nodes.name: 20-fold gain in instructions per bit
nodes.statement: Taken together, we achieve a gain factor of $5/2 \times 8 = 20$ in terms of instructions per input bits.
conclusions: we achieve a gain factor of $5/2 \times 8 = 20$ in terms of instructions per input bits

nodes.name: 16-bit words
nodes.statement: For simplicity, we focus on 16-bit words in this work.

nodes.name: wider words
nodes.statement: Wider words (larger universes) can be encoded into multiple distinct streams of 16-bit words. In addition, our algorithms can be generalized to wider words without difficulty.

nodes.name: scalar shift-mask-add positional population count
nodes.statement: To compute the positional population count, we start with sixteen zero-initialized bit-counters. Next, we iterate over the bits in each word in sequence while incrementing the corresponding target bit-counter as needed. A sensible baseline algorithm for computing the positional population count involves a shift-mask-add subroutine (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-naive}): \begin{enumerate} \item Right shift a 16-bit word by the bit index $p\in\{ 0,1,\ldots,15\}$. Mathematically, this is equivalent to an integer division by $2^p$ with the result being the integer quotient. \item Mask out all but the least significant bit from the shifted word. This bit is set when the quotient is odd, and zero otherwise. \item Increment the counter at position $p$ with the value from step 2.
nodes.statement_short: Baseline: for each 16-bit word and each bit index $p$, shift right by $p$, mask the LSB and add it to counter $p$.

nodes.name: scalar instruction estimate
nodes.statement: For sufficiently long input streams, we estimate the number of executed instructions to $\sim$4 per bit for a total of $\sim$64~instructions per 16-bit word.
conclusions: $\sim$4 per bit for a total of $\sim$64~instructions per 16-bit word

nodes.name: scalar cycle estimate
nodes.statement: Given that most recent Intel processors can retire four instructions per CPU cycle, we expect a processing speed of around 16~cycles per 16-bit word for this scalar shift-mask-add subroutine (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-naive}).
assumptions: most recent Intel processors can retire four instructions per CPU cycle
conclusions: we expect a processing speed of around 16~cycles per 16-bit word for this scalar shift-mask-add subroutine

nodes.name: CSA_AVX512 calls per network size
nodes.statement: We build CSA circuits over 512-bit registers using a CSA routine (Fig.~\ref{fig:csa-avx512}). The simplest network (Fig.~\ref{fig:hsillustration}) takes four 512-bit registers (or 256\,B) as inputs (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-avx512-small}) and uses three calls to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function. We can double the size of the network and process 512\,B inputs using seven calls to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function. Again, doubling the network size, we can process 1\,kB inputs using fifteen calls to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-avx512}).
conclusions: takes four 512-bit registers (or 256\,B) as inputs
uses three calls to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function
process 512\,B inputs using seven calls
process 1\,kB inputs using fifteen calls
nodes.statement_short: Networks over 4, 8, 16 registers (256 B, 512 B, 1 kB) use 3, 7, 15 AVX-512 CSA calls.

nodes.name: CSA network instruction counts
nodes.statement: Each call to the \texttt{CSA\_AVX512} function involves only two instructions (two times \texttt{vpternlogd}). Excluding load and store instructions, we use \begin{inparaenum}[(1)] \item 6~instructions per block of 256\,B or \item 14~instructions per block of 512\,B or \item 30~instructions per block of 1\,kB. \end{inparaenum} Notably, the number of instructions per input volume increases with wider circuits.
conclusions: 6~instructions per block of 256\,B
14~instructions per block of 512\,B
30~instructions per block of 1\,kB
nodes.statement_short: Networks cost 6, 14, 30 instructions for 256 B, 512 B, 1 kB blocks.

nodes.name: AVX-512 CSA positional population count
nodes.statement: At the end of each circuit, we have a set of registers \{\texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}, \ldots\} corresponding, for each bit position in $i\in [0,1,\ldots, 512)$, to the sum of set bits. For simplicity let us assume that we are working with the smaller circuit (256\,B). Before starting the procedure, the registers \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2} and the 16 output bit-counters are zero-initialized. Next, the first 512\,B of inputs are process with the circuit and receive as output the updated values of \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}. In addition, we also receive a new register \texttt{B3} corresponding to the fourth least significant bit of the sum of the set bits at position $i\in [0,1,\ldots, 512)$. We can update our sixteen bit-counters by checking the bits in \texttt{B3}: the first counter needs to be incremented by eight times the sum of the bits at indexes $\{0, 16, 32, \ldots, 496\}$, the second counter needs to be incremented by eight times the sum of the bits at indexes $\{1, 17, 33, \ldots, 497\}$, and so forth. The process of loading the next 512\,B of input data, call the circuit, and providing it with the updated values \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2} is repeated until no more data is available. At this point, when no more input data is available, we must increment our bit-counters with the remaining bits in \texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}. These are processed as \texttt{B3} except that the multiplier is 1, 2 and 4 respectively. The algorithms using the large circuits (512\,B and 1\,kB) work similarly.
nodes.statement_short: Run the AVX-512 CSA circuit over input blocks, carrying B0..B2; add weighted bit counts of the overflow register B3 to 16 counters per block, then flush B0..B2 at the end.

nodes.name: vectorized counter increment
nodes.statement: The inner loop of our algorithm, where the bit-counters from the \texttt{B3} register are updated could become expensive. This loop execute 16~sums of 32~bit values and multiply the result by eight. This final multiplication can be deferred until the end of the main loop. Further, we vectorize the sum (Fig.~\ref{fig:increment-avx512}) by using sixteen vector of counters, each spanning 512~bits, or thirty-two 16-bit counters, instead of using sixteen scalar counters. Given the \texttt{B3} register, we select the least significant bit of each 16-bit word by using a mask-select operation involving the \texttt{_mm512_and_si512} intrinsic function. Next, we increment counters using a horizontal add operation involving the \texttt{_mm512_add_epi16} intrinsic. Finally, we shift each 16-bit subword of the \texttt{B3} register right by one bit with the \texttt{_mm512_srli_epi16} intrinsic function.
nodes.statement_short: Defer the multiplication by eight and update sixteen 512-bit vector counters by mask-select, 16-bit add and right shift of B3.

nodes.name: total instructions per block
nodes.statement: By unrolling this vectorized code, we achieve $3 \times 16=48$~instructions, without considering overhead and load/store instructions. We can add these 48~instructions to our previous counts: \begin{inparaenum}[(1)] \item 54 instructions per block of 256\,B or \item 62 instructions per block of 512\,B or \item 78~instructions per block of 1\,kB.
assumptions: without considering overhead and load/store instructions
conclusions: 54 instructions per block of 256\,B
62 instructions per block of 512\,B
78~instructions per block of 1\,kB
nodes.statement_short: Adding 48 counter-update instructions gives 54, 62, 78 instructions per 256 B, 512 B, 1 kB block.

nodes.name: instructions per 16-bit word
nodes.statement: Dividing by the number of 16-bit words processed, we get the following instruction counts per word: \begin{enumerate} \item 0.42 when using blocks of 256\,B, \item 0.24 when using blocks of 512\,B, and \item 0.15 when using blocks of 1\,kB.
conclusions: 0.42 when using blocks of 256\,B
0.24 when using blocks of 512\,B
0.15 when using blocks of  1\,kB
nodes.statement_short: Per 16-bit word: 0.42, 0.24, 0.15 instructions for 256 B, 512 B, 1 kB blocks.

nodes.name: larger blocks perform better
nodes.statement: Based on these numbers, as block sizes get larger, we expect fewer instructions per input word and therefore improved performance.

nodes.name: >400-fold instruction reduction
nodes.statement: In comparison, we estimate about 64~instructions per 16-bit word for the scalar version. This corresponds to a $>$400-fold reduction in the number of executed instructions.
assumptions: we estimate about 64~instructions per 16-bit word for the scalar version
conclusions: This corresponds to a $>$400-fold reduction in the number of executed instructions.

nodes.name: overhead of recovering counts
nodes.statement: This analysis ignores the overhead cost of recovering the counts from both the vectorized counters and the running registers $\{\texttt{B0}, \texttt{B1}, \texttt{B2}, \ldots\}$. For small inputs, this overhead can occupy a dominant proportion of the total cost. For example, the sixteen vector counters span 1\,kB on their own. Hence, to achieve good performance, the input stream should at least exceed 1\,kB.
nodes.statement_short: Recovering counts from vector counters and B registers is a fixed overhead, so inputs should exceed 1 kB.

nodes.name: residual input handling
nodes.statement: Our SIMD-based approach can compute the positional population count for inputs that are a multiple of 256\,B. Any residual input values will be processed using a scalar subroutine.

nodes.name: performance independent of data
nodes.statement: However, we find that performance is independent of the input data as our algorithms do not branch on the content of the data.
conclusions: performance is independent of the input data
assumptions: our algorithms do not branch on the content of the data

nodes.name: fixed overhead for small inputs
nodes.statement: Our proposed AVX-512-based approach has a fixed overhead, irrespective of the input stream size. This overhead is non-negligible for small inputs. For tiny inputs (512~words), we need about 30~instructions per 16-bit word, and almost all of these instructions are part of the overhead. However, once we reach a few thousands words (e.g., 4096~words or 8\,kB), our AVX-512-based approach becomes beneficial.
conclusions: has a fixed overhead, irrespective of the input stream size
once we reach a few thousands words (e.g., 4096~words or 8\,kB), our  AVX-512-based approach becomes beneficial
nodes.statement_short: Fixed overhead dominates tiny inputs (about 30 instructions/word at 512 words); the AVX-512 method pays off from about 8 kB.

nodes.name: scalar speed is fixed
nodes.statement: For the scalar algorithm, we observe a fixed speed over the range of inputs in our experiments: 17~cycles and 65~instructions per input word.
conclusions: 17~cycles and 65~instructions per input word

nodes.name: 1 kB AVX-512 is fastest
nodes.statement: Overall, the fastest approach is our proposed AVX-512 algorithm with large block size (1\,kB), except maybe for inputs of less than 64\,kB.
conclusions: the fastest approach is our proposed AVX-512 algorithm with large block size (1\,kB), except maybe for inputs of less than 64\,kB

nodes.name: scaling with input size
nodes.statement: Increasing the input size reduce the number of instructions per input word and simultaneously increase speed. Due to diminishing returns, the performance for 1\,GB inputs are practically identical to that of 256\,MB.
conclusions: Increasing the input size reduce the number of instructions per input word and simultaneously increase speed

nodes.name: 300-fold fewer instructions
nodes.statement: In the best scenario, the AVX-512 approach uses 300~times fewer instructions compared to the scalar approach.
conclusions: the AVX-512 approach uses 300~times fewer instructions compared to the scalar approach

nodes.name: near memcpy speed
nodes.statement: As a reference point, the C \texttt{memcpy} function runs at a speed of 20\,GB/s for large inputs compared to 18 GB/s for the positional popcount operation on large inputs.
conclusions: 20\,GB/s for large inputs compared to 18 GB/s for the positional popcount operation on large inputs

nodes.name: Zero-initialize $B_0$ and $B_1$
nodes.statement: Starting with two 64-bit words initialized to zero: one for the least significant bits ($B_0$) and one for the second least significant bits ($B_1$).
nodes.statement_short: Zero-initialize $B_0$ and $B_1$

nodes.name: CSA of two inputs with $B_0$, carry $x$
nodes.statement: Two input words are summed with $B_0$ using a CSA subroutine (Fig.~\ref{fig:csacpp}) resulting in two outputs: one corresponding to the least significant bits stored in $B_0$ and another corresponding to the second most significant bit: let us call it $x$.
nodes.statement_short: CSA of two inputs with $B_0$, carry $x$

nodes.name: CSA of next two inputs with $B_0$, carry $y$
nodes.statement: Two new input words are summed with $B_0$ using the same CSA subroutine. Again the output corresponding to the least significant bit is stored in $B_0$. We have a second output corresponding to the second most significant bits, let us call it $y$.
nodes.statement_short: CSA of next two inputs with $B_0$, carry $y$

nodes.name: CSA of $x$, $y$, $B_1$ giving $B_1$, $B_2$
nodes.statement: In the final step, $x$, $y$, and $B_1$ are added together. The output corresponding to the least significant bits is stored in $B_1$. Similarly, the output corresponding to the most significant bit is stored in $B_2$.
nodes.statement_short: CSA of $x$, $y$, $B_1$ giving $B_1$, $B_2$

nodes.name: Build $F_{N+1}$ starting with $F_N$ on the first half
nodes.statement: We can then construct a larger circuit that takes twice as many inputs by two calls to the circuit together with an additional CSA routine. Indeed, to compute $F_{N+1} (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^{N+1}-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N})$, we can start by computing $F_N (d_0, \ldots, d_{2^N-1}; B_0, \ldots, B_{N-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Build $F_{N+1}$ starting with $F_N$ on the first half

nodes.name: Second call to $F_N$ on the second half
nodes.statement: We provide the first $N$~outputs ($B_0, \ldots, B_{N}$) from this first call to $F_N$ to a second call to the circuit $F_N$, this time using the $2^N$ following inputs $d_N, \ldots, d_{2^{N+1}-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Second call to $F_N$ on the second half

nodes.name: Combine the three $B_N$ values with one CSA
nodes.statement: We are left with three values $B_N$, one was provided as an input to $F_{N+1}$, and two have been produced by a call to the smaller circuit $F_N$. We can combine these with a CSA routine.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the three $B_N$ values with one CSA

nodes.name: Reduce to enumerating the 8 inputs
nodes.statement: This instruction is useful in computing the most and least significant bits in the CSA routine. To determine the value of the 8-bit sequence $i$ in the context of computing the least and most significant bits, it suffices to enumerate all 8~possible inputs (Table~\ref{tab:csatern}).
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to enumerating the 8 inputs

nodes.name: LSB is xor: immediate 150
nodes.statement: The least significant bit can be computed as the \texttt{xor} of the three inputs. Therefore, the \texttt{vpternlogd} instruction computes the desired output when the bits at index $\{1, 2, 4, 7\}$ of $i$ are set. In software, this bit sequence is represented as the integer 0b10010110 in binary or 150 in decimal.
nodes.statement_short: LSB is xor: immediate 150

nodes.name: MSB: immediate 232
nodes.statement: Computing the most significant bits involves the expression $(a \mathrm{~and~} b) \mathrm{~or~} ((a \mathrm{~xor~} b) \mathrm{~and~} c$. We can achieve this result by setting the bits at index \{3, 5, 6, 7\} of $i$ that can be represented as the binary string 0b11101000 or 232 in decimal.
nodes.statement_short: MSB: immediate 232

nodes.name: Zero-initialize sixteen counters
nodes.statement: we start with sixteen zero-initialized bit-counters.
nodes.statement_short: Zero-initialize sixteen counters

nodes.name: Loop over words and bit positions with shift-mask-add
nodes.statement: Next, we iterate over the bits in each word in sequence while incrementing the corresponding target bit-counter as needed. A sensible baseline algorithm for computing the positional population count involves a shift-mask-add subroutine (Fig.~\ref{fig:pospopcnt-naive}): \begin{enumerate} \item Right shift a 16-bit word by the bit index $p\in\{ 0,1,\ldots,15\}$. Mathematically, this is equivalent to an integer division by $2^p$ with the result being the integer quotient. \item Mask out all but the least significant bit from the shifted word. This bit is set when the quotient is odd, and zero otherwise. \item Increment the counter at position $p$ with the value from step 2.
nodes.statement_short: Loop over words and bit positions with shift-mask-add

nodes.name: Right shift by $p$
nodes.statement: Right shift a 16-bit word by the bit index $p\in\{ 0,1,\ldots,15\}$. Mathematically, this is equivalent to an integer division by $2^p$ with the result being the integer quotient.

nodes.name: Add bit to counter $p$
nodes.statement: Increment the counter at position $p$ with the value from step 2.
